newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: FOCUS - Austria says end near in Creditanstalt drama.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Austria says end near in Creditanstalt drama.

text.p: The final curtain fell in the six-year privatisation drama of Austrian bank Creditanstalt on Thursday when Austrian Finance Minister Klima said a decision on the sale would be made before New Year.

"The decision will probably be made between Christmas and New Year," Klima said, contradicting conservative Economy Minister Johann Farnleitner who earlier told reporters the sale would be wrapped up before the Christmas holidays.

Europe's longest running privatisation project took a nasty political turn last week when market leader Bank Austria emerged as the top bidder for the government's 19.9 million voting shares in Creditanstalt, reportedly offering more than 16 billion schillings ($1.4 billion) for control of the bank.
It is up against rival bids from a consortium led by Italian-controlled insurer EA-Generali and former supermarket tycoon Karl Wlaschek.

The ruling Social Democrats privately prefer Bank Austria's offer, while the conservative People's Party has openly opposed a sale of Austria's most blue-blooded bank to what is considered a socialist-led financial giant effectively controlled by the City of Vienna.

As the strain on the uneasy government coalition grew, Social Democrat Klima on Wednesday accused the conservatives of risking squandering tax payers' money if their desperate efforts to fend off Bank Austria were successful.
The People's Party has brandished a possible sale of Creditanstalt to Bank Austria as a "renationalisation", raising the prospect of a coalition breakup and a re-run of last year's snap elections.

Creditanstalt executives, lobbying behind the scenes, said the sale would constitute a "Soviet-style privatisation". Management claims Bank Austria is financially weak and say a link-up of the two would hurt Creditanstalt's image abroad.

Lawyers for the conservative-controlled group led by EA-Generali, which includes Germany's Commerzbank, Austrian savings bank Die Erste and Banca Commerciale Italiana, have threatened to ask the European Commission to investigate Bank Austria's bid.
The group claims Bank Austria's close ties to the City of Vienna, which guarantees the bank's liabilities, constitute a violation of European Union competition rules.

About 40 percent of the bank's capital is held by AV-Z foundation, which is effectively controlled by the City of Vienna. Some 17 percent is held by the state, while Germany's Westdeutsche Landesbank holds nine percent.

The People's Party upped the stakes in the politically fraught battle on Wednesday when they asked parliament to block a possible sale to Bank Austria, but the conservatives appeared unlikely to find the required parliamentary majority.
A similar motion by the far-right Freedom Party scheduled for Thursday was also seen as having few chances of success.

Last week the two voted together to urge the government to carry out a far-reaching privatisation of the nation's overcrowded banking sector. The Social Democrats rejected the motion as a "serious breach of the coalition agreement".
In a last-ditch effort at damage control, Social Democrat Chancellor Franz Vranitzky and conservative leader Wolfgang Schuessel said they would hold a meeting later on Thursday.
Bank Austria, meanwhile, called its Vienna-based staff for a closed evening meeting to outline its strategy. ($1=10.94 Schilling)
